newsitem.title: USA: Don't let budget take a vacation when you do.
newsitem.headline: Don't let budget take a vacation when you do.

text.p: You scrimp, save and control spending all year long to finance a well-deserved vaction.
But vacation memories can be spoiled when the credit card bill comes in and you see how much you really spent.
Some 230 million Americans are expected to take a vacation between June and August 1997. The average family of four, on a two-week U.S. vacation, will spend about $3,000 for food and lodging.
Add transportation and other extras -- including T-shirts, and other souveniers -- and the spending can be substantial.

Families who budget their expenses all year long tend to send budgeting on vacation as well when they take to the road, a Denver-based financial consultant said, leading to a bad case of receipt-shock when they return.
"Set a limit of what you want to spend. It's very important for the entire family to agree" before the vacation starts, said Becky Cutler, a Denver-based financial consultant.
"Being on vacation doesn't mean taking a vacation from managing your money," she said.
One of the greatest threats to vacation budgets is the use of credit cards. Many adults -- who pass this message on to their children -- think credit is an extension of money.
"It's a convenience," Cutler said, "that has to be repaid."

You don't have to pay for everything with cash, she said, but determine ahead of time how you are going to pay for specific expenses. For example, plan to put your motel bills and gas on a credit card, and spend cash on meals. That way, you can estimate what the credit card bill will be while setting limits on how much more you can spend using cash.

The little extras can really add up, and Cutler advises writing down every expenditure, no matter how small. The odds and ends, such as soft drinks, film and postcards, can accumulate, sending a budget into outer space.
Budgeting is not just for adults, Cutler said.

"Older children need to understand the limitations of money." Parents have to explain finances to their children "and have to learn to say no" when requests for money become excessive. Giving a child an allowance for the vacation is a good idea, making the child responsibile for selecting what souvenirs he or she wants and can afford.
"Parents have to set an example," Cutler said. "You can't tell kids you don't have much money, then spend a lot on a fancy dinner."
Here are some other tips on managing vaction spending, courtesy of Citibank's credit management education programme.
-- Set a limit on what you want to spend. Make this decision before you make vacation plans so you will take only a vacation you can afford.

-- Make a spending plan. Make a list of what you think your major expenses will be, such as transportation, lodging and food, and estimate the costs. Deduct these amounts from your overall vacation budget to detertime how much you have left over for day-to-day activities. Divide the amount by the number of days in your vacation to get a daily spending allowance.
-- Keep track of spending. Write down every expenditure, no matter how small, and add it to your daily tally to make sure you stay within your budget.

-- Choose your "way to pay" carefully. One can use cash, personal checks, travelers checks, credit card and debit cards. If taking a credit card along for emergency use only, make sure there is a sufficient credit allowance.
-- Make vacation spending a family affair. Get everyone involved in the budget-making process and avoid impulse purchases.
-- Save money by taking a vacation at home. You don't have to travel afar for a vacation.

"If you don't have money for a long vacation, maybe short weekend trips, or stay home and go to movies, sporting events, the beach or amusement area. Kids often have creative ideas that don't cost a lot of money," Cutler said.

-- Save receipts and spending records. When the vacation is over, review your spending to see if you accurately estimated your expenditures and stayed within your budget. This year's spending can give you a realistic starting point for next year's vacation spending plans.
